guide_passage:
The protector does not have to disappear. It may remain watchful while willingly allowing one small step, provided you remain present and able to stop. If it says no, don’t turn that into permission.
Then follow what changes. A critic may soften into a fear; a vague hurt may become a specific need; anger may clarify a boundary that needs action. Respond to what has become available instead of restarting the original exercise. When a need becomes clear, try offering that kind of care and notice how it lands. You don’t need an age, a recovered memory, or a complete cast of parts to work with a feeling. A useful shift may be small; more intensity is not the only way forward.
length: five to eight sentences, 70 to 100 words
brief:
- the last paragraph of the new h3 "Hear the Protective Part First" (the guide's A Bottom-Up Sequence), right after the paragraph above. It takes the place of two paragraphs that failed and repeated the article, so it carries only what's new, briefly.
- what it has to carry, in meaning: that protective part doesn't have to go anywhere. It can keep watch while you try one small step, as long as you're still present and could stop, and if it says no, that's a no. Then watch what changes. One example is enough: a critic that kept putting this down might turn out to be scared, and that's easier to be kind to. Answer whatever shows up right where it is, instead of starting over to look for your little one. If a need gets clear, try offering that kind of care and notice how it lands. A small shift counts.
- Joel, 2026-10-04: it's "about breaking up the instruction manual flow, which requires some kind of within-the-thought reflection or jumping", because "people will gloss over fast if everything is one long stepwise instruction sheet". At each step ask how a human author would re-engage the reader right there: an aside to the reader in the middle of a thought, a quick reaction, a jump to a picture. His own fixes in this h3 did it with "(hopefully, right?)" after the roommate's move-in speech, "Peek-a-boo!" right after your little one comes forward, and "Even if you didn't win an Emmy last year" before a convincing performance. Those show the kind of move; don't reuse them.
- No list of three or more in one sentence. Call it "that part" or "a protective part", never "the Protector" (the grown-up's own function here).
- Every sentence has to work for a reader who doesn't remember anything sections back.
